title: Is this KIIFB's end? Sudha Pillai committee wants life support withdrawn
content: The Report of the Committee formed to review the Kerala Infrastructure Investment Fund Board (KIIFB) has called for the virtual shutdown of the LDF government's innovative infrastructure funding mechanism. The Committee, chaired by former finance secretary Sudha Pillai, has asked the UDF government to unplug the two entitlements that have till now pumped life into KIIFB. One, the obligatory annual transfer of motor vehicle tax and petroleum cess from the state budget to the KIIFB account. And two, it authority to raise funds from the market. The Committee wants both these rights immediately cancelled. The Committee wants the infrastructure works already initiated by KIIFB to be taken over by the concerned departments. "The funds required for completing these projects shall be provided as capital expenditure in the Annual Budget over the next five years, beginning in 2026-27," the Committee report, which was tabled in the Assembly on Thursday, said. It also recommended an urgent performance audit of KIIFB for a period of ten years from 2016-17. Till June 30, 2026, 24,764.64 crore has been transferred to KIIFB from the state budget. Of this, 19,404.52 crore was motor vehicle taxes, and 5038.04 crore was petroleum cess. The government has also contributed an additional 322.07 crore. Unspoken dangers The Committee revealed a hidden cost of such budgetary transfers. The report said that the daily cash outflow from the consolidated fund to KIIFB "depresses the State's minimum balance with the Reserve Bank of India and increases the frequency and duration of recourse to Special Drawing Facility (SDF) and Ways and Means (W&M) Advances and, beyond those, to Overdraft (OD)". In short, such obligatory transfers deprive the state of necessary funds in a crisis. Moreover, such crisis borrowing from the RBI comes with a price; penal rates are involved. "Every rupee of additional recourse caused by the escrow outflow (the fund flow to KIIFB) therefore carries a cost that is additional to, and entirely separate from, the coupon (interest) KIIFB pays on the underlying borrowing," the report says. The state, in effect, pays twice. "Once through the interest embedded in KIIFB's borrowing, and again through the carrying cost of the liquidity it surrenders to service that borrowing (which is the penal rate imposed by the RBI on the state for drawing more than its daily limit to make up for the money pumped into KIIFB)." The bonds issued by KIIFB also pose a future risk. The outstanding value of these bonds is 8,649.97 crore. The maturity profile shows that repayment will touch 1,236 crore a year between 2029-30 and 2032-33 on the bond portfolio alone. Here's the shock. It is still not clear how this money will be paid back. "No consolidated plan covering the redemption of the bond portfolio alongside bank and institutional repayments was placed before the Committee by either KIIFB or the Finance Department, notwithstanding that the liability falls substantially on the State," the Committee notes. Why CAG was right The Committee also agreed with the CAG's earlier finding that KIIFB's borrowings were not a contingent liability as claimed by the government, but a direct charge on the state's revenues. The CAG wanted KIIFB's debts to be reflected in the state's budgets. Now, the Sudha Pillai Committee has also recommended the same. Here is why the Committee came to such a conclusion. The CAG data shows that the government transferred 11,869.28 crore to KIIFB from 2021-22 to 2024-25. In the same period, KIIFB's debt service (principal plus interest) was 11,944.18 crore. "The transfers therefore equalled 99.4 per cent of debt service. In other words, over the period for which comparable data exist, virtually the entire flow of State tax revenue into KIIFB was consumed by servicing KIIFB's own borrowings...
